note.note:
Consult Summary:
- Acute viral upper respiratory infection (common cold) with dry cough and nasal symptoms; managed with supportive care; no prescription needed; monitor for worsening or persistent symptoms.

History:
- Presenting complaint: Cough and runny nose for several days.
- Onset/duration: Symptoms began approximately five days ago, around the start of the weekend; course ongoing.
- Symptom details: Dry, hacking cough; nasal congestion/runny nose; muscle aches; occasional headaches; chills; mild throat redness.
- Exposures/exacerbating factors: No noted exertional dyspnea or chest tightness; no wheeze.
- Associated symptoms: No blood in sputum; no shortness of breath; no fever reported.
- Pertinent negatives: No sore throat with tonsillar enlargement; no cervical lymphadenopathy; lungs described as not wheezy or rattly; breathing currently normal.
- Self-care measures: Uses over-the-counter analgesics as needed; previously took paracetamol; ibuprofen not used.
- Pertinent positives: Mild oropharyngeal redness; throat examined with no significant tonsillar enlargement; normal chest findings on exam.

Past Medical History:
- Type 2 diabetes mellitus, on metformin for several years (approximately 5–6 years).
- Hypertension, on lisinopril.
- Regular home blood glucose monitoring; blood pressure reportedly normal on the most recent reading.

Medications:
- Metformin (dose/route/frequency not documented).
- Lisinopril (dose/route/frequency not documented).
- Paracetamol (dose/route/frequency not documented) for symptom relief.
- Night Nurse / Day Nurse (OTC cough/cold remedies) (dose/route/frequency not documented).

Allergies:
- Not documented.

Social History:
- Not documented.

Family History:
- Not documented.

Physical Examination:
- Vitals: Blood pressure reported as normal earlier today; numeric values not provided. Other vitals not documented.
- General/HEENT: Mild redness at the back of the throat; no enlarged tonsils; no palpable neck glands.
- Chest/Lungs: No wheeze or rattling sounds; patient breathing normally; no signs of chest infection.
- Other: No acute cardiopulmonary distress noted in the exam as described.

Investigations:
- None ordered or reported.

Assessment & Plan:
- Overall Impression:
  - Primary: Acute viral upper respiratory infection (common cold) with dry cough; no evidence of pneumonia or acute lower respiratory infection on exam.
  - Supporting context: Cough and rhinorrhea for ~5 days; mild throat redness; stable breathing; no SOB or abnormal lung sounds.

- DDx Integration (brief):
  - Acute viral upper respiratory infection (common cold)
    - Supporting: Cough, rhinorrhea, mild throat redness, absence of respiratory distress, normal exam.
    - Opposing: Aches and chills could occur with influenza; no fever documented.
  - ACE inhibitor–induced cough
    - Supporting: Lisinopril use; dry, hacking cough.
    - Opposing: Timeline unknown; symptoms also fit viral URI; no clear medication change history.
  - Acute bronchitis
    - Supporting: Persistent cough after URI symptoms.
    - Opposing: No lung findings (no wheeze/crackles) and exam largely benign.
  - Influenza
    - Supporting: Myalgias/chills reported; cough and systemic symptoms possible.
    - Opposing: No fever documented; illness appears milder and more typical of a common cold.

- Issue 1: Acute viral URI (primary diagnosis)
  - Plan:
    - Reassurance and supportive care.
    - Over-the-counter relief with Night Nurse / Day Nurse as tolerated; current medications not contraindicated.
    - No antibiotics or prescription required at this time.
    - Return precautions: seek medical attention if shortness of breath develops, wheezing occurs, or symptoms persist >3 weeks or worsen.

- Issue 2: ACE inhibitor–associated cough (consideration)
  - Plan:
    - No immediate change to lisinopril; monitor symptoms.
    - If cough persists or becomes burdensome, reconsider evaluation with PCP to assess for ACE inhibitor–related cough (recognizing this is a potential alternative diagnosis).

- Issue 3: Acute bronchitis (consideration)
  - Plan:
    - No antibiotics given; monitor for any new focal lung findings or symptoms suggesting bacterial infection.
    - If symptoms evolve (new fever, dyspnea, chest pain), reassess and consider further evaluation.

- Follow-up:
  - If symptoms persist beyond 3 weeks or worsen, contact clinic for re-evaluation and possible chest examination.

- General plan items:
  - Continue diabetes management as usual; maintain home glucose monitoring.
  - No current prescriptions needed beyond OTC remedies.
  - Maintain hydration, rest, and symptomatic care.
